articles.title: Livestreamed intimacies: Parasocial production and labour in the K-Pop industry
articles.abstract: This article investigates how the emerging technology of livestreaming is a productive medium to facilitate parasociality – the one-sided sense of intimacy and relational bonding by audiences to media figures – and how this has been strategically implemented by the South Korean idol industry’s (‘K-Pop’) business model. Anchored to the case study of BTS’s livestream activities, we propose this developing area of scholarship as a new textual medium of ‘livestreamed intimacies’. The paper argues that livestreaming efficiently produces experiences of intimacy and thus facilitates parasocial relationships through its shared temporality, limited cinematographic form, and asymmetrical interactivity. We observe how BTS’s 2020-2023 livestreams trend towards late night, candid broadcasts in private settings, implicating labour boundaries. With continued pursuit for parasocial productions, this paper infers that with increased adoption and expansion of technology, livestreaming is heightening the commodification of relationship cornerstones such as intimacy, authenticity, and the private within the entertainment industries.

articles.title: Scrolling through tensions: Work-related memes and the discursive construction of tensions in digital work
articles.authors: Camilla Aarnio, Ward van Zoonen, Anu E. Sivunen
articles.abstract: Organizational life is increasingly characterized by tensions and paradoxes, intensified by digitalization and changing conditions of work. This study examines how Internet memes reflect, reproduce, and perform these tensions within contemporary digital work discourse. Drawing on a qualitative multimodal analysis of work-related memes shared on Instagram, we explore how irony, intertextuality, and participatory meaning-making articulate contradictions of working life. Situating memes within broader shifts in digital labor—such as algorithmic mediation, precarity, and expectations of constant availability—we apply an integrative framework for analyzing organizational oppositions. Our findings identify recurring tensions, including agency–inertia, expression–inexpression, rationality–irrationality, and hypocrisy–integrity, which converge around an overarching tension of control and resistance. We show how memes function as multimodal, participatory sites of paradoxical category work through which tensions of digital work are simultaneously contested and normalized.

articles.title: Genre as infrastructure: Power, platforms, and the governance of musical classification
articles.abstract: Discussions surrounding musical genres frequently commence with the assertion that these categories undergo evolution and defy rigid definitions. This article posits that the core issue extends beyond evolution to encompass governance: the institutional and platform-driven mechanisms through which musical diversity is identified, solidified, disseminated, and monetized. Utilizing genre theory, cultural sociology, infrastructure studies, and platform studies, this work reconceptualises musical genre as a form of regulatory infrastructure rather than merely a neutral descriptor. It critiques the notion of stable origins and demonstrates how the concept of “original genre” is frequently constructed retrospectively through markets, archives, curricula, and canons. It subsequently analyses streaming platforms like Spotify and Apple Music, where genre is defined through metadata, recommendation systems, behavioural clustering, and audio modelling. Expanding upon the concepts of algorithmic culture, listener practices, and hybrid gatekeeping, particularly in relation to the streaming paradox, this argument posits that genre is increasingly defined by metrics: categorized, grouped, ranked, curated into playlists, recommended, and assessed within the frameworks of platform infrastructures. African musical formations, such as highlife, Afrobeats, Ghanaian art music, and Pentecostal worship music, illustrate the tendency of global taxonomies to oversimplify intricate musical ecologies into generalized categories like “world” or “African.” The article presents a Layered Stabilisation Model that includes historical core, institutional codification, and adaptive circulation. It contends that genre scholarship ought to transition from a focus on definition to one of governance.

articles.title: Can democracy speak under AI-driven visibility? Toward an affective–algorithmic reworking of the spiral of silence
articles.abstract: This article offers a critical theoretical reassessment of the conditions shaping political expression and its boundaries within algorithmically mediated publics, examining how artificial intelligence–driven infrastructures of visibility, intertwined with affective dynamics, alter the conditions under which opinions acquire public presence and come to be perceived as legitimate to express. The argument is illustrated through a case-based analysis of highly visible user interactions surrounding posts by the Portuguese populist leader André Ventura across Facebook, TikTok and X, which serves to explore how different socio-technical environments give rise to distinct climates of opinion. Revisiting the Spiral of Silence theory from the perspective of contemporary platform environments, the article argues that silencing is no longer adequately explained primarily through interpersonal fear of isolation, but must instead be understood as emerging from the interplay between algorithmically structured visibility and affectively charged interaction. On this basis, the article reconceptualises the Spiral of Silence as an affective–algorithmic process and contributes to debates in communication theory and digital political communication, while asking whether, and under what conditions, democracy can still be said to speak when publicness itself is algorithmically organised.

articles.title: Increasing the effectiveness of health communication advertising
Sentiment distribution bias in AI-generated review summaries
articles.authors: Fei Wang, Zhecheng Liu, Fang Wang, Zhen Zhu, Shan Wang
articles.abstract: Purpose E-commerce platforms increasingly deploy generative AI (GAI) to summarize large volumes of customer reviews. This study examines sentiment distribution bias in platform-provided GAI review summaries, defined as distortion in the relative representation of positive, neutral and negative sentiment compared with their proportional presence in the associated review corpus. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in information theory, we characterize four sentiment distribution bias patterns and develop an input-output framework linking source review characteristics and summary design features to sentiment bias. We analyzed data from an online travel platform covering 847 Tokyo hotels with GAI review summaries linked to 111,115 customer reviews to assess sentiment bias and conducted a complementary experiment to examine downstream consumer responses. Findings The platform's GAI review summaries exhibited predominant positive bias: positive sentiment was overrepresented, whereas neutral and negative sentiments were underrepresented relative to the review corpora. Lower source review volume, higher rating entropy and lower positive imbalance were associated with greater sentiment bias, whereas longer summaries, greater attribute granularity and lower attribute sentiment diversity were associated with lower bias. An experimental study showed that, relative to a low-bias summary, a GAI review summary with greater positive bias improved consumers' attitude toward the hotel and increased booking intention, despite being perceived as less helpful. Originality/value This research documents sentiment distribution bias in platform-provided GAI review summaries, identifies input and output conditions under which such bias varies and examines its consequences for consumer responses. The findings extend the online review and GAI literatures while informing platform governance and responsible GAI deployment.

articles.title: When are imperfections beneficial? The impact of aesthetic imperfections in virtual and human influencers on consumer engagement
articles.authors: Min Tian, Zhenyu Li, Sigen Song
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to resolve a key paradox in influencer marketing: why brands are increasingly designing virtual influencers with aesthetic imperfections (e.g. freckles), despite conventional wisdom suggesting that perfection is key. It investigates when and why these imperfections enhance consumer engagement, specifically by comparing their effects on virtual versus human influencers. Design/methodology/approach The research employs two main experiments and a supplementary robustness study. Participants were exposed to images of either a virtual or a human influencer, both manipulated to have aesthetic imperfections. The data were analyzed using ANOVA and a moderated mediation model to test the proposed theoretical framework. Findings The two main studies show that aesthetically imperfect virtual influencers elicit higher consumer engagement than aesthetically imperfect human influencers, partly through perceived scarcity. A supplementary study further rules out perceived authenticity and anthropomorphism as alternative mediators and shows that the effect extends to purchase intention, especially under symbolic product appeal framing. Practical implications Brands can enhance virtual influencer engagement by using minor aesthetic imperfections as scarcity cues, especially for consumers seeking uniqueness and symbolic products. Originality/value This study compares consumer responses to aesthetic imperfections in virtual and human influencers. It helps reconcile mixed findings in the literature and advances theory by identifying perceived scarcity as a psychological mechanism that enhances virtual influencer appeal. The study also extends scarcity theory to the digital context and offers practical guidance for designing “perfectly imperfect” virtual personas that engage targeted consumer segments.

articles.title: Sneezers or catchers of shock among green cryptocurrencies, energy cryptocurrencies and Bitcoin Gold: an R-squared decomposed connectedness
articles.authors: Miklesh Prasad Yadav, Pratiksha Jha, Shakeb Akhtar
articles.abstract: Purpose To analyze shock transmission, shock absorption and systemic interconnectedness in decentralized cryptocurrency markets by examining how structural differences across cryptocurrency subcategories (green, energy and Bitcoin Gold) influence contagion dynamics and network resilience. Design/methodology/approach This study employs an R-squared decomposed connectedness approach to investigate contemporaneous and lagged spillovers among eight cryptocurrencies that have been classified as green (Cardano, XRP, Polygon and Stellar), energy-centric (Powerledger, Electrify Asia and Sun Contract) and Bitcoin Gold for the period ranging from December 31, 2019 to July 22, 2024. It evaluates directional shock transmission (“TO”), shock absorption (“FROM”) and net connectedness to identify the role of individual assets as transmitters and receivers within the network. Additionally, hedge ratios and portfolio weights are calculated to offer insights into diversification potential and hedging effectiveness across cryptocurrency subcategories. Findings The findings indicate a high degree of systemic interconnectedness among closely linked decentralized networks. Contemporaneous connectedness is more pronounced than lagged connectedness, indicating rapid information diffusion within cryptocurrency platforms. Network diffusion analysis identifies Stellar and Cardano as net transmitters (sneezers), and Sun Contract and Electrify Asia as net receivers (catchers), exhibiting systemic risk elevation and diversification capabilities, respectively. Originality/value This study contributes to Information Systems research by integrating digital contagion theory and a socio-technical perspective into the empirical analysis of cryptocurrency platforms. It introduces network-based decomposition of connectedness to differentiate between immediate and persistent contagion and offers one of the initial empirical analyses of heterogeneity across cryptocurrency subcategories. This study connects infrastructure design with contagion dynamics and provides innovative perspectives on governance-by-design, network resilience and systemic vulnerabilities in developing a digital ecosystem.

articles.title: When platforms integrate generative AI: the dynamics of professional contribution in artist communities
articles.authors: Keyu Cui, Shan Liu, Chenze Wang, Yang Liu, Xiaoxiao Liu
articles.abstract: Purpose Generative AI (GAI) is transforming user-generated content (UGC) communities, yet its impact on professional creators remains underexplored. This study examines how the platform-level integration of a GAI illustration tool into an online artist community influences designers' original content contributions and how these effects vary by designer characteristics. Design/methodology/approach We use 12 months of panel data on 43,587 active designers from a leading online creative platform. Leveraging the platform's introduction of a free GAI illustration tool in October 2022 as a natural experiment, we employ a difference-in-differences design to estimate its effect on designers' original work postings. Findings The results indicate that integrating the GAI tool increases original content contributions by 25%. This effect is driven by multiple mechanisms, including competitive pressure, learning-oriented engagement, and copyright concerns. In particular, competitive pressure induces strategic effort reallocation, leading designers to reduce contributions within their primary domains and shift effort toward less-affected creative areas. Moderation analyses further show that this reallocation effect is stronger among newer and lower-reputation designers. Originality/value Amid growing interest in the impact of GAI, this study centers on the creative domain, shifting the focus from GAI's influence on creative processes to its effects on professional content contributions in online communities. It identifies key mechanisms – competitive pressure, learning-oriented engagement, and copyright concerns – arising from platform-level GAI integration. The findings provide theoretical and practical insights for managing creative platforms in the era of GAI integration.

articles.title: Redundant Reference as an Interactional Resource: Social Situation and Recipient Familiarity in Referential Choice
articles.authors: Xiaoxiao Lu, Sibei Ye, Siyun Liu
articles.abstract: In interpersonal communication, speakers often provide more information than is minimally necessary for referent identification, thereby producing redundant reference. Although such expressions have often been treated as cooperative, less is known about whether, and how, they are systematically shaped by social-interactional considerations. The present research addressed this question through three language-production experiments examining the joint effects of visual scene characteristics (color and number of distractors) and social-interactional factors (social situation and recipient familiarity) on redundant reference. Across the three experiments, redundant reference emerged not as mere informational excess, but as an adaptive referential strategy jointly shaped by referential information demands, social situations, and recipient familiarity. Together, these findings provide empirical evidence for understanding redundant reference as a flexible referential choice from a social-cognitive perspective.

articles.title: Covariation in Attachment Orientations and Support and Strain Across Multiple Relationships Over Time
articles.authors: William J. Chopik, Aislinn E. Low, Isabella S. Stephanoff, Hyewon Yang, Annika S. Jaros
articles.abstract: Attachment orientations describe how individuals think, feel, and behave in close relationships, yet little research has examined how these orientations vary over short time periods and as a function of different relationships. In this study, 938 emerging adults completed three surveys across two months assessing attachment anxiety and avoidance, along with perceived support and strain from friends, parents, and romantic partners. Using multilevel modeling, we separated between-person and within-person variance to examine whether relationship experiences predicted both average levels and short-term fluctuations in attachment orientations. Between-person analyses showed that individuals reporting higher average support across relationship types also reported lower attachment anxiety and avoidance. Greater strain—particularly from parents and friends—was linked to higher attachment anxiety, on average. Within-person analyses revealed that higher levels of perceived support (relative to one’s typical levels) were associated with concurrent lower levels of attachment avoidance. Strain, in contrast, was not a consistent within-person predictor. These associations typically generalized across friends, parents, and romantic partners. These findings suggest that attachment orientations fluctuate alongside changes in relational experiences over relatively short periods of time. The magnitude of these fluctuations was consistent across relationships—potentially expanding the avenues through which attachment security can be promoted.

articles.title: Adult Adoptees’ Perceptions of the Impact of Memorable Messages About Religion and Adoption
articles.authors: Emily J. Helder, Kayla DeVries, Haley Kranstuber Horstman, Jade Henness, Zachary Davis, Rachel Grimes, Elizabeth Lam, Grace Arakelian, Chloe Warren, Kendal Lyssy
articles.abstract: This qualitative study explored adult adoptees’ perceptions of the impact of memorable messages about religion and adoption that they received while growing up in Christian adoptive families. Situated within the theory of memorable messages, the research examined the perceived impact of these memorable messages on adoptees’ relationships, identity development, emotional well-being, and religiousness. Forty-one adult adoptees participated in semi-structured interviews regarding religious memorable messages about adoption, such as being chosen , saved/rescued, adoption being part of God’s plan , and described the perceived impact of receiving these messages from adoptive family and church members while growing up. The majority of participants perceived negative or difficult impacts of the messages, such as inauthentic or alienated family relationships, barriers to adoptive or racial identity development, and emotional difficulties. Additionally, in response to these messages, participants reported a need to renegotiate relationships with religion and religious communities, either by holding on to parts of religion while letting go of messages they had been told or by cutting ties with religion entirely. Conversely, a minority described religious memorable messages as emotionally comforting, faith-affirming, celebrating of their identity, and leading to a deepening of relationships. Overall, adoptees’ retrospective sense-making seemed to shape their perceived impact of messages, supporting the theory of memorable messages’ emphasis on interpretive processes over time. The findings contribute to scholarship on adoptee identity formation and emotional well-being. Additionally, findings related to estrangement and factors contributing to religious disaffiliation have implications for the broader literature on these topics across various family forms.

articles.title: Adult Attachment Predicts Parental Empathy: Evidence Across Four Samples of Parents of Children From Preschool Through Middle Childhood
articles.authors: Jessica A. Stern, Bonnie E. Brett, Jacquelyn T. Gross, Tracy Riggins, Jude Cassidy
articles.abstract: Extensive research points to the importance of adult attachment in predicting empathy, but little research has examined the role of attachment in shaping adults’ empathy specifically for their children. This paper examines how adult attachment avoidance (discomfort with emotional closeness) and attachment anxiety (worry about abandonment by relationship partners) contribute to empathy within parent–child relationships. Across four studies, we test these links using a multi-dimensional, multi-sample approach, drawing on data from parents of children spanning preschool (Studies 1 and 2), school-age (Study 3), and middle childhood (Study 4), with a total of 349 parents of children ages 3–10 years. In each study, parents completed the Experiences in Close Relationships scale and the Interpersonal Reactivity Index—Parent version, adapted to assess parents’ empathy for their child (i.e., parental empathic concern, perspective-taking, and personal distress), alongside a range of other empathy measures. Controlling for child sex and maternal education, analyses consistently showed that attachment avoidance was associated with parents’ lower empathic concern and, for parents of preschool-aged children, lower perspective-taking; in contrast, results for attachment anxiety were mixed and often null. In addition, longitudinal analyses (Study 1) revealed that attachment avoidance at baseline predicted relative decreases in parental perspective-taking over a 4-month period. Both attachment anxiety and avoidance showed nonsignificant associations with parents’ personal distress after accounting for covariates. Findings have implications for attachment theory, relationship science, and parenting interventions.

articles.title: The Distinct Roles of Rejection Sensitivity and Disconnection/Rejection Schema in Fear of Intimacy: A Longitudinal Study of Young Adults
articles.authors: Cuiping Mou, Tingting Li, Jie Shi, Cancan Jin
articles.abstract: Young adulthood is a critical period for the development of intimate relationships, yet fear of intimacy may interfere with the formation and maintenance of close romantic bonds. Previous studies have linked early interpersonal experiences to fear of intimacy, but many have relied on retrospective measures or cross-sectional designs, limiting conclusions about temporal associations. To address these limitations, the present study examined whether rejection sensitivity was involved in the prospective association between disconnection/rejection schema and fear of intimacy, and whether perceived social support moderated this pathway. Data were collected from 236 young adults (82.6% women; age range = 17–32 years, M age = 21.41) across a four-month interval. After controlling for baseline levels of rejection sensitivity and fear of intimacy, the overall longitudinal moderated mediation model for total fear of intimacy was not supported. Exploratory dimension-specific analyses suggested a more differentiated pattern: rejection sensitivity was associated with fear of losing the other, whereas disconnection/rejection schema was directly associated with fear of losing the self. The conditional indirect effect through rejection sensitivity emerged only at high levels of perceived social support; however, because the interaction effect was not statistically significant, this finding should be interpreted cautiously. These results suggest that different dimensions of fear of intimacy may be associated with distinct psychological processes. The findings also underscore the importance of using autoregressive controls and more rigorous longitudinal designs when examining mechanisms underlying fear of intimacy.

articles.title: Emotional Clarity of Others but Not Self Relates to Extrinsic Interpersonal Emotion Regulation
articles.authors: Jocelyn Lai, Angie M. Gross, Wesley Tucker, Tammy English
articles.abstract: In close relationships, individuals manage each other’s emotions (interpersonal emotion regulation [IER]). Emotional clarity of oneself (EC-self) is a key individual difference in the management of emotions and maintenance of well-being. Recent work has examined the relational benefits of emotional clarity of others (EC-others). However, less is known as to whether EC-self or EC-others have unique associations with relational behaviors, as well as intrapersonal ER (i.e., regulation of one’s own emotions) and extrinsic IER (i.e., regulation of other’s emotions). We leveraged two studies of friendship in emerging adults (Study 1 [S1] N = 674; Study 2 [S2] N = 374). In S1, EC-others was related to more positive and less negative friendship behaviors. Further, EC-others but not EC-self was associated with more emotionally supportive and less dismissive IER strategies (e.g., receptive listening, valuing, distraction, suppression). In S2, EC-self was associated with intrapersonal ER (less difficulty and greater perceived success in regulating one’s own emotions), while EC-others was associated with both intrapersonal ER (greater frequency, effort, and difficulty in regulating one’s own emotions) and IER (less perceived difficulty in helping a friend feel better). Findings suggest EC-self’s relevance for intrapersonal processes and EC-others’ importance for both intrapersonal and interpersonal processes.

articles.title: “I Can Feel that You Love Me”: Approximating Affectionate Touch in Long-Distance Romantic Relationships
articles.authors: Jason A. Mitala, Sarah E. Dickerson, Brett K. Jakubiak
articles.abstract: Affectionate touch is beneficial for romantic relationships, but some couples (e.g., those who are long-distance) cannot physically touch. In this project, we introduce “touch-adjacent behaviors,” gestures that approximate affectionate touch without physical contact. We demonstrate that “mimed touch” (i.e., acting out touch; e.g., blowing kisses over video chat) and “expressed touch” (i.e., statements that convey touch through language; e.g., texting “I wish I could hug you”) are utilized by long-distance partners and are endorsed as a form of perceived compensation for relationship distance. We also characterize the people most likely (e.g., those who use other forms of affection) and least likely (e.g., avoidantly attached individuals) to use these behaviors. Finally, we establish that mimed and expressed touch co-occur with relationship quality and provide preliminary evidence that these links are stronger for people with higher attachment avoidance. This research suggests touch-adjacent behaviors are common and potentially beneficial in long-distance relationships.

articles.title: Examining Support Received and Changes to Spousal Caregivers’ Social Convoys Across the Dementia Disease Trajectory
articles.authors: R. Amanda Cooper, Karen Shalev, Lily G. Gorman, Ida Ghaemmaghamfarahani, Chizobam Nweke
articles.abstract: The social convoy model suggests that an individual’s support network includes their closest relational connections and more distal relationships that provide support. These networks, called social convoys, shift across the lifespan but might also change during stressful life events such as providing care for a person with dementia. We conducted retrospective interviews with 18 dementia spousal caregivers to examine changes in their social convoys while caring for their partners. We found that at dementia onset, caregivers’ social convoys included their spouse, family and friends, and broader community members who provided direct support, indirect support, and/or unsupport. Caregivers’ social convoys changed as dementia progressed: some family/friends moved closer while others left the social convoy altogether, formal care moved closer in the convoy, and spouses with dementia moved from supporters to co-recipients of support. Our analysis has implications for social convoy literature and practical implications for spousal caregivers and dementia clinicians.

articles.title: Children’s Differential Susceptibility to Peer Acceptance and Rejection: A Multi-informant Longitudinal Study
articles.authors: Danni Liu, Anouk van Dijk, Maja Deković, Judith Semon Dubas
articles.abstract: In this multi-informant longitudinal study, we examined whether children with higher levels of self-reported sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) showed stronger longitudinal associations between peer relationships (i.e., peer acceptance and rejection) and their social-emotional functioning (i.e., prosocial behavior, aggressive behavior, and emotional symptoms). Participants were 567 third- and fourth-grade children ( M age = 9.16 at Wave 1; 58.8% boys; 98.9% Han Chinese), followed across three waves, spaced one year apart. Peer acceptance and rejection were measured using classmate nominations at Waves 1 to 3, SPS through children’s self-reports at Wave 3, prosocial and aggressive behaviors through both mother reports and classmate nominations at Waves 1 to 3, and emotional symptoms through mother reports at Waves 1 to 3. Results revealed only one significant SPS moderation effect among the many tested, providing little evidence for SPS-based differential susceptibility in this context. We discuss explanations, including study-level constraints and broader theoretical questions, such as whether person-centered approaches may better capture distinct susceptibility subtypes that may emerge by late childhood.

articles.title: “Love’s Sweet Exile”: Manic Street Preachers’ Richey Edwards Between Intimacy and Ideology
articles.abstract: The present writing examined the life and work of musician Richey Edwards (1967-went missing 1995, declared deceased 2002), guitarist and chief lyricist for the Welsh rock band Manic Street Preachers from 1989 until his disappearance six years later. The study paired the functionalist emotion theory with more recent research to formulate a developmental psychology of love that incorporated both the social and the romantic under a single conceptual rubric. Edwards spent his adolescence and early adulthood attempting to form a clique that would constitute a private world free from the compromises of society. This quest led Edwards into joining Manic Street Preachers in 1989. The band’s success, however, seemed to hasten Edwards’ plunge into anxiety, self-harm, and anorexia. The study found that Edwards’ inability to forge intimate relationships led him to become an overachieving secondary school student, after which he became the leader of an ideologically driven peer group that eventually became a musical ensemble. Society’s version of love, as well as the conventional version of romantic love, were both sidestepped by Edwards’ self-appointment as the revolutionary ascetic of the English music scene. Unfortunately, Edwards’ mental state deteriorated during the nineties, leading to his commitment to a mental hospital and finally to his probable suicide in 1995. The study concluded that Edward’s peculiar life strategy was an attempt to use his membership in a rock band as a social bottleneck that would allow him to criticize the realms of vocational, familial, and romantic love without being infected with their demands. On the positive side, Edwards produced a body of work that continues to enthrall and inspire listeners; on the negative side, his unacknowledged need for intimacy led him down the darkest of paths.

articles.title: The Roles of Source Citations in Identifying Misinformation and Disinformation: Moderating Effects of Digital Literacy and Information Types
articles.authors: KyungWoo Kim, Seungheon Han, Sung-Bou Kim, Ha Hwang
articles.abstract: This study investigates whether source citations enhance detection of false information and whether their effects depend on digital literacy and information processing style. In an experimental survey of 1,013 South Koreans, citations show no overall effect. However, they significantly improve detection of disinformation—but not misinformation—among individuals with higher digital literacy. Intuitive processing lowers detection ability, and citations do not counteract this tendency. The findings challenge assumptions that transparency universally improves evaluation, showing that citation effectiveness depends on user capabilities and the type of falsehood, and highlighting the need to strengthen digital literacy alongside transparency initiatives.

articles.title: Book Review: Insights on Broadcast Journalism by Keeble, R. L., & Mair, J. (Eds.) KeebleR. L.MairJ. (Eds.). Insights on Broadcast Journalism. Routledge, 2026. 212 pp. ISBN: 9781032983202 (hbk); ISBN: 9781003598077 (ebook).
The Trouble With Catching Up: Problematizing the “AI Gap” and its Global Inequities in Journalism
articles.abstract: The “artificial intelligence (AI) gap” in journalism describes a divide between newsrooms equipped to innovate and benefit from AI and those left behind. Rather than an objective condition, this study examines this gap as a discursive construction, drawing on articulation theory. Using the JournalismAI Academy for Small Newsrooms as a case study, we combine ethnographic observation with interviews conducted in 2022 to 2023 and 2025. Findings demonstrate how technological lag is articulated as a problem and AI investment as its solution, a linkage stabilized through assumptions of inevitable, linear technological progress—legitimizing particular ways of thinking about and acting on AI.

articles.title: Contradicting Epistemic Inequalities: The Case of the Journalist Navina Sundaram
articles.abstract: This contribution asks how social inequalities are perpetuated through colonial silences maintained through practices of knowledge production in journalism. Drawing on postcolonial scholarship, it examines how these silences have historically been challenged between the 1960s and 1980s. Based on documents from the personal files of Navina Sundaram, one of the first non-White journalists on West German television, it traces the practices of contradicting that challenge and uphold journalistic epistemology: contradicting visibility in editorial practices, contradicting through international networks, and denying belonging. Together, these practices show how debates on diversity in German journalism are rooted in historical struggles for epistemic justice.

Multi-Method Analysis of Locally Built Artificial Intelligence Models Designed for Journalists in an African Country
articles.authors: Adeola Abdulateef Elega, Abdullateef Mohammed, Akintunde Babatunde
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models for journalism have been built within the Global North context, hence deepening the concerns of the “AI divide” between the North and South. This has compelled organizations in various areas of the Global South to develop journalism-focused AI models to address the specific challenges peculiar to journalism practice within the region. Nigeria stands out within the Global South context because organizations are developing local AI models to empower local journalists. However, the extent to which these AI products can address real-life journalistic challenges is unknown; hence, this study assesses how well locally developed AI models are positioned to support journalists in Nigeria, using a purposive sample of four homegrown tools: ChatJourno, Dubawa Chatbot, ChatVE, and MyAIFactChecker. Employing a mixed-methods design, we conducted walkthrough usability tests by engaging 15 trained journalists who provided rigorous assessments of the functionalities of each tool. We then conducted semi-structured interviews with the developers of each of the tools to assess each platform’s vision and directly cross-check those claims against the test-users’ evidence. Findings show the tools generally aim to complement Nigerian newsroom needs, such as improving news drafting and accelerating verification, but their realized value is uneven. While some of the platforms offer usable interfaces and services, some common limitations include gaps in up-to-date data and unusable features. We conclude that the tools must reliably achieve their promised functions because usability strongly drives user acceptance, and mass newsroom adoption will follow only when tools demonstrably enhance content standards in news practice.

articles.title: Bounded Watchdogging: Platform Governance, Risk Structures, and the Reconfiguration of Science Journalism
articles.authors: Liu Yang, Qixin Lin, Zhongxuan Lin
articles.abstract: This article examines six cross-platform biomedical research-integrity controversies in mainland China to analyze how open-source investigation becomes integrated with journalistic verification under platform governance. Drawing on a research design that combines multiple qualitative methods such as digital trace ethnography, process tracing, and semi-structured interviews, the study identifies a four-stage process of science watchdogging: initial disclosure, verification and evidence accumulation, media intervention, and institutional response. This process shows how journalists use open-source information to conduct investigative science reporting. Building on these findings, the article further proposes a model of bounded watchdogging organized around trade-offs among speed, verifiability, and risk, showing how public-facing online leads and digital traces can be transformed into journalistic evidence. In this way, the findings not only offer journalists a practical verification pathway for producing science investigations, but also extend watchdog journalism theory beyond liberal-adversarial assumptions in the Chinese context.

articles.title: Not Afraid of AI yet: Indonesian TV Journalists on Negotiating Roles in AI-Assisted Newsrooms
articles.authors: Yearry Setianto, Rossalyn Asmarantika, Veronika, Angela Romano
articles.abstract: The introduction of Indonesia’s first AI-generated news presenter by tvOne in 2023 marked a symbolic moment in the country’s experimentation with AI in television journalism. While AI adoption has sparked global debates about automation and the future of journalistic labor, less is known about how journalists themselves interpret these technologies, particularly in Global South media environments. This study examines how Indonesian television journalists make sense of AI in newsroom practices through the lens of journalistic role perceptions. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 television journalists from 12 national newsrooms, the findings indicate that journalists largely perceive AI as a supplementary tool to assist routine production tasks rather than replace core journalistic functions. Participants purported that video capture, editorial judgment, contextual interpretation, and verification remain irreplaceably human responsibilities in television news. These interpretations reflect the continued importance of established journalistic roles, particularly information dissemination and accountability, in shaping television journalists’ responses to technological innovation. Simultaneously, journalists’ views are embedded within broader structural conditions, including economic pressures and newsroom restructuring in Indonesia’s television industry. This study demonstrates how journalists negotiate AI adoption by balancing professional values with the changing economic realities of television news production.

articles.title: AI in Cameroonian Newsrooms: Exploring Daily Use and Challenges Among Journalists in Four Regions
articles.abstract: This study examines the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools by journalists working for legacy media outlets in four of Cameroon’s 10 geopolitical regions. It builds on the premise that journalism practice is continually changing due to the advent of emerging technology. The article analyses semi-structured interviews with 12 Cameroonian mainstream media practitioners working for public and private print- and broadcast-media outlets. The unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (Venkatesh et al., 2003) serves as the theoretical lens through which the actions of the research participants are analyzed. Findings reveal that some journalists use AI throughout all stages of their work, from conception, planning, collection, writing, and editing. The extent of use depends on the individual reporter’s ability to leverage the tools. The attempt to take full advantage of AI tools is met with significant challenges, such as the absence of appropriate newsroom policies, resource limitations, the absence of context-relevant data, and insufficient knowledge among newsroom managers. The study emphasizes that the adoption of technology in newsrooms cannot be separated from the socio-economic context in which media operate.

articles.title: AI Adoption in Indonesian and Malaysian Journalism: A Comparative Mixed-Methods Study
articles.authors: Indra Prawira, Mastura Mahamed, Tai Neilson
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping journalistic practice worldwide, automating tasks such as transcription, translation, content generation, data analysis, and personalisation. News organisations across the Global South are also experimenting with public-facing applications of AI, including AI-generated anchors and reporters. These developments challenge assumptions about technological lag in non-Western newsrooms, revealing how competitive pressures, resource constraints, and platform dependency can drive distinctive modes of technological adoption. This article compares Indonesian and Malaysian journalists’ attitudes toward AI and their intentions to integrate these technologies into their professional practice. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods approach grounded in the technology acceptance model, the study analyses how perceived usefulness, ease of use, and social norms influence decisions about the adoption of AI in news production. While both countries demonstrate strong links between usability and perceived value, cross-national differences in how these measures influence adoption intentions highlight how local contexts inflect journalists’ attitudes. Interviews further reveal that acceptance is shaped not only by individual attitudes but by policy, market dynamics, infrastructure, generational dynamics, and anxieties about technological displacement. This article advances the study of individual journalists’ attitudes toward AI within a critical, contextually grounded approach to technological adoption.

articles.title: Does alternative news media inform or misinform voters during election campaigns?
articles.authors: Atle Haugsgjerd, Rune Karlsen, Tine Figenschou, Karoline Andrea Ihlebæk, Toril Aalberg
articles.abstract: A growing body of literature has studied the audiences and effects of alternative media use. We contribute by examining how such usage shapes political knowledge during election campaigns. Given their partisan orientation, lack of professional verification, and often provocative style, alternative media are found to produce and circulate misinformation, even as their users are often politically engaged, active news consumers. We ask whether alternative media inform rather than misinform citizens during election campaigns. Adopting a two-dimensional conception of political knowledge, we examine both surveillance knowledge and confidence in that knowledge – along with misinformation understood as the combination of the two. Utilizing individual-level panel data from Norway, our findings suggest that alternative news use is not associated with being better or worse informed, but with being more confident in one’s political knowledge. We discuss how these effects may differ in more polarized or lower-quality information environments.

articles.title: The intended and unintended affordances of post-separation parenting apps
articles.abstract: Little research has examined the role of specific technologies in relationships characterised by unequal power, such as those which underpin post-separation domestic and family violence. Drawing on the mechanisms and conditions framework of affordances and the methods of feature analysis, this study analyses 32 post-separation parenting apps along with in-depth interviews with 18 Australian victim–survivors who used these platforms with a perpetrator. We identify intended outcomes embedded in app design and contrast them with unintended outcomes emerging in practice. Analysis revealed that the design and promotional materials of the apps influence their use as a reinforcer of litigious mindsets and actions. This combination appears to change user behaviours, leading to communication becoming anticipatory and strategic with mixed outcomes.

articles.title: #BlackExcellence and #BlackGirlMagic are for all of us: Black influencers’ rejection of neoliberal logics and post-feminist discourses of entrepreneurship
articles.abstract: Situated within feminist media communication studies, this project uses critical technocultural discourse analysis to examine how #BlackExcellence emerges as a form of “digital Black practice” among Black women influencers and users. This study is framed within the context of the George Floyd protests in 2020 and 2021 as mainstream media outlets appropriated Black Excellence rhetoric in columns, listicles, and videos following this watershed moment. Analyses of popular press articles about Black influencers, discourse about race and labor on #BlackTumblr, influencer content on Instagram and YouTube, and interviews with Black influencers comprise the dataset. By leveraging intersectional platform affordances and racialized erotic capital, Black influencers subvert neoliberal and post-feminist logics undergirding digital labor by virtue of the racialized work they are expected to perform, challenging exceptionalist rhetoric. I argue that Black influencers’ uniquely racialized, gendered work contests the assumption that influencer labor is a natural outgrowth of neoliberal conditions.

articles.title: Audible, Spotify, YouTube & Co.: The German Digital Audiobook Market in the Context of Platformization
articles.abstract: This article examines the contemporary digital audiobook through the lens of platformization and develops a conceptual framework for understanding platformized audiobook culture. Drawing on an integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship, supplemented by market reports, industry statistics, and audience studies, it uses the German audiobook market as an analytically illuminating example through which broader processes of platformization can be explored. The article situates audiobooks within wider transformations of everyday digital media practices, highlighting the shift from physical formats toward downloads and subscription-based streaming services. Conceptually, it distinguishes platformized audiobook culture from digital audiobook culture through two complementary analytical perspectives adapted from book studies, digital publishing, and media and communication studies: an integrative platform model and a data-environment model of streaming services. Building on this synthesis, the article proposes an ecosystem model of platformized audiobook culture to support future theoretical and empirical research.

articles.title: Brand governance in the platform economy: From political to regulatory recognition
articles.abstract: This article reconceptualises corporate advocacy as brand governance, a techno-normative promotional practice that regulates the conditions of political visibility within networked publics. Drawing on a sociosemiotic analysis of global advocacy campaigns (2017–2022), the analysis identifies three strategies, Visionary (“Feeling the Other”), Sensitive (“Feeling for Others”) and Reflexive (“Feeling with Others”), each operating through distinct affective and narrative logics. The argument advances a distinction between political and regulatory recognition. Political recognition acknowledges claims in their structural and collective dimension; regulatory recognition extends legitimacy only to claims aligned with the promotional regime’s affective and reputational logic. The evidence suggests that brand governance operates predominantly in this regulatory mode, producing a conditional visibility that privileges individualised emotional appeals over structural political demands. This study focuses on US and Western European promotional cultures; comparative research across other regions remains a necessary next step.

articles.title: A Preliminary Test of the Comprehensive Model of Post‐Dissolution Distress: Predicting Initial and Over Time Changes in Distress Following Romantic Dissolution
articles.authors: René M. Dailey, Zhengyu Zhang, Lingzi Zhong, Kyle Kearns, Sarah Varga, Sooyong Lee
articles.abstract: This study provided a preliminary test of the Comprehensive Model of Post‐Dissolution Distress with longitudinal data. The model includes distal (static; e.g., breakup controllability, relational anxiety) and proximal (time‐varying; e.g., desiring reconciliation, coping, quality of alternatives) factors in predicting both initial distress and change in distress over time. Adults who had experienced a breakup in the past 30 days completed an initial survey and were invited to complete 5 monthly follow‐up surveys. Analyses ( N = 272) showed that a set of distal and proximal factors significantly contributed to explaining 66% of the variance in initial distress. Relational anxiety, desiring reconciliation, and self‐medicating coping more consistently predicted change in distress over time for those who remained single across the timepoints ( n = 143). This model can be utilized in theory‐building to understand how the factors work collectively to predict post‐dissolution distress and highlight proximal factors that can be altered to alleviate distress. With the limited statistical power, additional research replicating and extending these findings would be beneficial.

articles.title: Children's Perception of Interparental Conflict Scale: Development and Validation of the Japanese Version and Its Short Form
articles.authors: Yasumitsu Jikihara, Shunsuke Suzumura, Akiko Hirose, Satoko Ando
articles.abstract: This study developed and provided initial validation evidence for a Japanese version of the Children's Perception of Interparental Conflict Scale (CPIC‐J) and a more efficient short form (CPIC‐JS) for Japanese older adolescents. Two independent samples of Japanese high school students aged 15–18 years ( N = 335; data collected December 2022–January 2023) completed the translated CPIC and measures of emotional security and adjustment. Competing structural models were evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis, including higher‐order and bifactor formulations, and the consistency of the measurement model across the two samples was examined. To create the short form, items were selected within each original subscale using graded response modeling and expert review to preserve content coverage while reducing participant burden. The best‐fitting model had a bifactor structure characterized by a relatively strong general IPC appraisal factor and more limited domain‐specific factors. CPIC‐J and CPIC‐JS scores exhibited theoretically consistent associations with emotional security and adolescent adjustment indicators, supporting convergent and criterion‐related validity. Findings indicate that the CPIC‐J provides a culturally appropriate tool for assessing adolescents' perceptions of interparental conflict in Japan, whereas the CPIC‐JS may offer a low‐burden alternative for large‐scale surveys and settings requiring brief assessment; however, domain‐level scores should be interpreted cautiously.

articles.title: Does Order Matter? The Impact of Methodological Decisions in Survey Research Concurrently Examining Attachment to Mothers and Fathers
articles.authors: Ariane J. Gauthier, Natalie Kirby, Jean‐François Bureau, Audrey‐Ann Deneault
articles.abstract: While questionnaires are often validated in a context where participants respond to a questionnaire only once, it is common to complete a given questionnaire multiple times referring to different relationships in interpersonal relationship research. For instance, in attachment questionnaires, participants frequently respond to a given questionnaire for both their mother and father. Yet, it is unknown if the order in which these questionnaires are administered influences their validity. The present study explored this question by manipulating the administration condition of the questionnaires and the order in which participants reported on their relationship with each parent. A sample of 1046 undergraduate students (72.9% women) responded to online questionnaires on attachment and mental health. Results indicated that the experimental manipulations did not influence participants' engagement in insufficient effort responding, nor did they substantially impact internal consistency, observed scores, and questionnaires' factorial structure. Examining the correlation comparisons indicated that administering the mother and father versions of attachment questionnaires either side by side or completely sequentially might yield the most accurate correlations between parents and attachment questionnaires. Multigroup path analyses also suggest that administration condition and order of presentation influenced some associations between attachment dimensions and mental health symptoms, potentially impacting criterion validity.

What methods make possible: Reflections on methodological innovation and theory building in public relations
Politics, power, and professional practice: Cultural control in an Indian political public relations department
Reimagining public understanding: Toward an institutional model
articles.abstract: Public understanding of science is often framed as either factual knowledge or generalized trust in experts. This article advances an alternative: an institutional model, grounded in cultural awareness of the norms, practices, and boundaries through which science produces credible knowledge. Existing approaches struggle to distinguish scientific controversy from broader social conflict, limiting their ability to explain why science’s legitimacy falters in politicized contexts. An institutional perspective instead shifts the focus from individual deficits to science’s role as a social system—embedded in tensions between expertise, politics, industry, and democratic accountability. We outline the implications for science communication and public engagement, arguing that meaningful participation requires not only understanding science’s institutional role in civic life but also the capacity to evaluate scientific actors against cultural expectations and normative commitments. The article concludes by proposing a research agenda centered on the cultural meaning of science and how its credibility depends on public evaluation.

articles.title: Stop pushing junk science! User corrections of misinformation in science are common and sophisticated
articles.abstract: Misinformation is often equated with blatant falsehoods from dubious sources, overlooking that scientific sources, too, can accidentally publish inaccurate information to large online audiences. This article explores how social media users share, evaluate and address misinformation in science, defined as unreliable research rejected by relevant experts for violating scientific integrity. Using a mixed-methods analysis of Twitter discussions on retracted COVID-19 studies (33,730 tweets and 13,743 replies), the study found that, while most users accepted retracted science at face value, they were also disputed often, with user corrections accounting for nearly half of all replies. Corrections also closely mirrored established experimental recommendations, being mostly elaborative, non-confrontational, and commonly employed one or more debunking strategies. In contrast, polarising and overly convoluted language was rare. The results highlight the significant role that ordinary users play in countering unreliable science ‘in the wild’ and the need for researchers and policymakers to strengthen support for bottom-up corrective practices.

articles.title: The structural contingency model of trust: When variability in perceived trustworthiness of scientists signals critical support
articles.abstract: Prevailing approaches to measuring public trust in scientists rely on facet averages that overlook within-person variability, a dimension traditional views equate with ambivalence or attitudinal weakness. This study introduces the Structural Contingency Model of Trust (SCMT), proposing that the functional meaning of this variability is contingent on an individual’s overall trust level. In a Bayesian analysis of survey data from 68 countries ( N = 69,534), higher Trust Level (mean across 12 facets) strongly predicted greater general confidence in scientists. Critically, a credible interaction effect supported the SCMT: among highly trusting individuals, greater Trust Variability (variance across facets) was associated with the highest probability of reporting a great deal of confidence in scientists. This Critical Support profile suggests that variability can signify robust, differentiated engagement rather than evaluative weakness, offering a nuanced framework for understanding the complex, multidimensional nature of public trust in scientists.

articles.title: Sharing the Alternative – The Role of Digital Platforms for Alternative News-Sharing Behavior
articles.abstract: In a time of growing concerns over factual accuracy in the public sphere, alternative news media have emerged as a counterpoint to traditional mass media. In Germany, many online-only outlets cater to a rising audience, driven by distinct goals, standards, and funding structures compared to what they term ‘elite media’. Digital platforms are vital to their success, enabling audience growth with minimal financial investment and bypassing legacy media systems’ critique and verification mechanisms. Their reach, however, relies on followers sharing content and leveraging social media’s network effect to amplify niche information. Yet, the sharing habits of alternative news audiences remain understudied. This study uses original survey data from over 2,000 German alternative news users (collected in September 2023), exploring whether these patterns drive alternative media’s rise as a counterweight to established journalism. We investigate users’ sharing activity, their motivations for sharing news or refraining from it, and sociodemographic/ideological predictors for alternative news sharing.

articles.title: “Fairness Labels” in Feeds: Process Disclosures, Provenance, and User Choice Among Short‑Video Creators in Mainland China
articles.abstract: Algorithmically ranked feeds allocate attention in ways that can reproduce inequalities in visibility. We test whether a compact, feed-level process disclosure —a banner describing exposure-safeguard governance, paired with provenance cues and in-situ user-choice affordances—improves perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy among short-video creators in mainland China. In a mobile-first online experiment with 1,154 research-verified PRC creators in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), participants viewed a realistic feed randomized to No label , Personalization notice , or Fairness disclosure ; within the fairness condition, we factorially varied frame (Safeguards/Parity/Quotas/Exposure-fairness), issuer provenance (platform vs. independent audit), and disclosure depth (minimal badge vs. brief rationale). The compound fairness disclosure increased perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy relative to both controls and was accompanied by lower self-censorship and higher voice intentions. Effects were directionally stronger in civic/news contexts and among creators who self-identified as marginalized or previously down-ranked. Within-arm exploratory diagnostics suggested that quota-like parity framing may yield directionally lower legitimacy than exposure-fairness framing, while audit cues produced directionally positive but imprecise trust gains. Backfire checks found no implied-unfairness spillover for unlabeled items and no interaction with per-item AI-content labels, although AI labels reduced perceived accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that governance-aligned micro-disclosures can function as procedural visibility signals for creators, while underscoring the importance of verifiable claims and careful disclosure design.

articles.title: Narratives of Power: AI, Agency and the EU AI Act
articles.abstract: Public debate around AI has been characterised by hegemonic narratives that delineate the scope of the conversation, suppressing different voices and limiting nuanced discussion of the technology’s harms and benefits. Scholars have identified technological or enchanted determinism, the arms race mentality and the utopia versus dystopia debate as key narratives around AI. These ideas saturate the conversation, driven primarily by the tech industry, which positions itself as the (only) expert voice. The industry’s capacity to drive these narratives is facilitated by its established institutional authority and dominant presence in public discourse, as well as the knowledge asymmetry inherent in the proprietary, ‘black-box’ nature of AI systems. Tech firms leverage the technical opacity of AI and their powerful societal position to define the contours of public debate, assigning agency to AI itself and the tech industry; constructing users and civil society as passive observers or recipients; and establishing a frame for debate that focuses on extreme consequences or hyperbolic benefits. This study, conducted early in 2024, investigates the effects of this interpretive frame on the policy choices and communications of the EU AI Act, through a mixed-methods computational and critical discourse analysis. Within EU governing body texts, the same discursive patterns that map agency and erase the middle ground of debate in AI are found, helping to marginalise alternative perspectives from other stakeholders and prevent nuanced understandings of potential harms. In the context of the Act itself, these patterns reverberate in the assignment of agentic roles and the scope of the regulation.

articles.title: Incivility Among Politicians: Driven by Rational Minds or Personal Drives?
articles.abstract: There is growing concern about politicians engaging in incivility by mocking and insulting each other. While prior research often explains such discourse through rational choice, emerging work highlights the role of politicians’ individual traits, such as their personality. Yet, a unified theoretical account of how rationality and individual predispositions interact to shape harmful elite discourse is lacking. Drawing on foundational insights from psychology, we argue that politicians’ discourse reflects primarily rational considerations, which are moderated by their individual predispositions, leading to uncivil communication between politicians. We test this notion using elite survey data, unobtrusive measures of their individual traits, and direct observations of politicians’ social media communication in Belgium – a rare integration of psychological and behavioral evidence at the elite level. The results show that politicians’ use of uncivil discourse responds to rational considerations, but that the strength of this response depends on their individual predispositions. These findings demonstrate that individual traits moderate how politicians translate rational incentives into harmful discourse, providing a more nuanced account of the causes of elite incivility.

articles.title: Policy Window as a Trapdoor: Rethinking the Multiple Streams Framework through the Defunding of U.S. Public Media
articles.authors: Hilde Van den Bulck, Christopher Ali, Jonathan Kropko
articles.abstract: This article analyses the 2025 defunding of U.S. public media as a critical case to revisit Kingdon’s multiple streams framework (MSF). While MSF offers a useful heuristic for understanding policy change through the convergence of problem, policy, and political streams, its explanatory power is limited by assumptions of contingency, pluralism, and stakeholder inclusion. Under growing illiberalism, the “policy window” functioned less as an accidental opening than as a trapdoor, built through ideological persistence, institutional erosion and coordinated policy design. Drawing on critical discourse analysis of congressional hearings, executive orders, political communication, and media coverage, alongside survey data on public broadcasting system audiences, this study shows how conservative actors sustained a politicized definition of public media bias and institutionalized policy solutions. The survey highlights a disjuncture between audience trust and the construction of public media as a policy problem. Rather than spontaneous convergence, the case reflects coordinated restructuring of the public media system. More broadly, it suggests that MSF becomes less effective when stream independence is undermined by executive dominance and ideological alignment, requiring approaches that foreground power, discourse, and exclusion.

articles.title: An Effort Made for Whom? Exploring Ministers’ Public Approval and Name Recognition in Relation to Their Media Activity
articles.authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Jonas Krogh Madsen, Peter Heyn Nielsen
articles.abstract: In many democracies, cabinet ministers find themselves in a difficult situation, juggling a demanding administrative job with political responsibilities and the need to communicate and campaign to secure reelection. With the rise of social media, this balance is becoming increasingly unstable. However, the tangible benefits of media visibility outside election campaigns remain unclear, making it difficult to determine whether such efforts yield meaningful political returns. This study examines and compares whether Danish ministers’ media activities—both in traditional and social media—impact their name recognition and popularity in the Danish population. We utilize thirty-two nationally representative opinion polls conducted between March 2020 and May 2024 and merge these with extensive records of all Danish ministers’ Facebook activity and appearances in traditional media outlets throughout the same period. Overall, our findings show that ministers’ activity in traditional media is associated with only minor gains in name recognition, while social media activity has either zero or minimal gains in popularity. Moreover, breaking down these correlations across different types of Facebook interactions and traditional media outlets suggests a trade-off between reaching and being perceived favorably by voters, showing the multifaceted nature of (social) media activity. Consequently, while we do not rule out any significant effects of social media on voters’ perceptions, we argue that social media activity is no panacea for politicians to improve their public popularity and name recognition.
